clue.text: Noble ran madly to put the funeral flag straight

indicators.note: running madly suggests these letters going wildly out of order

explanation.surface: A nobleman dashes off in a frenzy to straighten a flag at a funeral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges NOBLE and RAN; 'to put ... straight' fits the surface and adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A banderole is a small streamer, notably one carried at a funeral and draped over a tomb.

clue.text: The cause of those ursine sore heads? Just fancy!

definitions.text: The cause of those ursine sore heads? Just fancy!

parts.words: The cause of those ursine sore heads? Just fancy!
parts.note: read literally as insects that pester bears and give them the proverbial sore head, but really an imagined terror, a thing of fancy

explanation.surface: A whimsical guess at why bears are always grumpy.
explanation.definitionFit: An object of baseless dread or persistent annoyance, originally an imaginary hobgoblin, so a product of fancy.

parts.note: a cow's hoof, boiled to make jelly, is literally the part of the animal that goes down to the earth

explanation.surface: A practical, unpretentious cook who makes jellies.
explanation.definitionFit: The hoof of an ox (neat being old for cattle) yields a gelatinous stock used for jelly.

indicators.note: the word me is placed inside the word for an end

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be put right at last.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct its errors.

parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the weaver Bottom says 'odious' where he means a word for sweet-smelling, and is corrected

explanation.surface: Something the character Bottom found hateful.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom, the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, rehearses 'Thisby, the flowers of odious savours sweet', and Quince corrects him.
explanation.definitionFit: Odorous means having a scent, the word Bottom garbled into 'odious'.

clue.text: Favourite of the boys' club, the little dear !

parts.note: Pop is the elite prefects' society at Eton College
a favourite is a pet

explanation.surface: A child who is the darling of a boys' club.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop is the self-electing society of senior boys at Eton, the English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: A poppet is an affectionate term for a small, sweet child or loved one.

parts.note: reads as guidebooks for tourists, but describes both collected volumes and public road vehicles that carry passengers

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both large collected editions of books and passenger buses.

clue.text: One sounds like fun for the marriage-broker

indicators.note: the clue says the word is heard like another

parts.note: a party is a bit of fun

explanation.surface: Someone who sounds amusing to a matchmaker.
explanation.walkthrough: A parti is a person regarded as a good match; 'for the marriage-broker' says whose view this is.
explanation.definitionFit: A parti is a person considered as an eligible marriage prospect, someone a matchmaker would rate.

parts.note: reads as an artist's gifts, but also recalls the old sense of a stroke of the pen or brush

explanation.definitionFit: Distinguishing characteristics; the word once also meant a stroke of a pencil or brush.

parts.note: bird is slang for a young woman, and this one tended the sacred fire in Rome

explanation.definitionFit: A Vestal virgin was a priestess who kept Vesta's sacred fire burning in ancient Rome.

clue.text: A line from the Duchess in the bar

definitions.text: A line from the Duchess in the bar

parts.words: A line from the Duchess in the bar
parts.note: a duchess is addressed as Her Grace, so a short letter from her, found in a musical bar

explanation.surface: A duchess sends a note while drinking in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A duchess is styled 'Your Grace'; the bar is a measure of music, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornamental extra note added to a melody, which appears within a bar of music.

indicators.note: made of, so the lady's name is formed out of the letters of the next word

explanation.surface: The lady who presides over a country manor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a weak signal here: the name is made of the letters of MANOR rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is a woman's name, and the heroine of Bellini's opera.

clue.text: " Tell thy grief ; It shall be if France can yield relief" (3 Hen. VI)

definitions.text: " Tell thy grief ; It shall be if France can yield relief" (3 Hen. VI)

parts.words: " Tell thy grief ; It shall be if France can yield relief" (3 Hen. VI)
parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 3 with one word missing, to be supplied from the play

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare promising help from France.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means relieved or lessened, fitting a grief that French aid will soften.

parts.note: reads like an award, but names a supporter of a political party named after the tenth month

explanation.surface: An award given to the best party worker each month.
explanation.walkthrough: The Octobrists were a Russian constitutional party formed after the Tsar's October Manifesto of 1905.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Russian party founded on the October Manifesto of 1905.

clue.text: There's a diamond in the fish !

definitions.text: There's a diamond in the fish !

parts.words: There's a diamond in the fish !
parts.note: reads as a jewel found inside a fish, but the word for the diamond shape was also the old name for the turbot

explanation.surface: Someone cuts open a fish and finds a gem.
explanation.definitionFit: An equilateral parallelogram is a diamond shape, and Rhombus was a former generic name for turbot-like fish.

clue.text: "It is a — evening, calm and free " (Wordsworth)

definitions.text: "It is a — evening, calm and free " (Wordsworth)

parts.words: "It is a — evening, calm and free " (Wordsworth)
parts.note: the opening line of a Wordsworth sonnet with its adjective left out

explanation.surface: A line of Wordsworth describing a peaceful evening.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a poetic form meaning lovely, the adjective Wordsworth used of the evening.

parts.note: a lass is a girl
OS stands for outsize, very big

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a man landing a tall woman.
explanation.walkthrough: OS (outsize) is a clothing abbreviation for very large sizes.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy's lariat traps animals, so as a verb it means catches with a noose.

parts.note: reads as beginning a task, but means to bring something into being

explanation.definitionFit: To give rise to or begin something, to be the source of it.

clue.text: Says it all over again about conditions

parts.note: re means about or concerning
states are conditions

explanation.surface: Someone repeats their account of the circumstances.
explanation.definitionFit: To repeat something stated before, saying it afresh.

clue.text: Hats that are liable to be clutched at

definitions.text: that are liable to be clutched at
definitions.meaning: a drowning man clutches at these, the idiom for desperate hopes

explanation.surface: Hats that people grab at in a gust.
explanation.definitionFit: Boater hats are made of dried stalks, and desperate people proverbially clutch at slender hopes of the same name.

clue.text: Sailor among drunks in heavy shoes

indicators.note: the sailor is placed among the drunks, inside them

parts.note: sots are drunkards
AB is an able-bodied seaman

explanation.surface: A sailor drinking with drunkards while wearing clumpy footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Sabots are wooden clogs, heavy footwear once worn by French peasants.

clue.text: Maiden, I have a letter here

parts.note: a miss is a maiden, an unmarried girl
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A young woman announces she has brought a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A missive is a written message, especially a long or formal one.

definitions.meaning: the superlative of meet, an old word for suitable
the archaic second-person form of the verb to meet, to encounter

explanation.surface: An archaic remark that it is proper for you to cross over.
explanation.definitionFit: Meet means suitable, so its superlative is most suitable; it is also the old second-person form of meet, encounter.

clue.text: What Sir. Joseph Porter advised the ambitious to do to their desks?.

definitions.text: What Sir. Joseph Porter advised the ambitious to do to their desks?.

parts.words: What Sir. Joseph Porter advised the ambitious to do to their desks?.
parts.note: in HMS Pinafore the First Lord tells those who would rise to stick close to their desks and never go to sea

explanation.surface: Career advice from a character in a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Joseph Porter is the First Lord of the Admiralty in Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore, who sings 'Stick close to your desks and never go to sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick fast or cling to something, as Porter urged clerks to cling to their desks.

clue.text: Having much to be said on both sides

definitions.text: Having much to be said on both sides

parts.words: Having much to be said on both sides
parts.note: describes a question with strong arguments for and against

explanation.surface: A question with strong arguments for and against.
explanation.definitionFit: Open to argument or dispute, with no settled answer.

parts.note: Br. abbreviates British, a nationality
an awl is a tool for boring holes

explanation.surface: A tedious citizen is caught up in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' looks like a dull person; it is the verb, giving a hole-boring tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl is a noisy fight or row.

parts.note: the phrase 'do you get my ...' means do you understand, and Rorke's is the start of a famous battle site

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person named Rorke has been understood.
explanation.walkthrough: Rorke's Drift was an 1879 battle in the Anglo-Zulu War; 'get my drift' means understand my meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Drift is the general meaning of what is said, and also a ford, as at Rorke's Drift.

indicators.note: being full of drink scrambles these letters like a drunken mind

explanation.surface: A gambler who has drunk too much cider.
explanation.definitionFit: A dicer plays at dice, a gambler.

clue.text: Muse who has time to make a speech

parts.note: an era is a period of time
taken as written

explanation.surface: A goddess of inspiration finds time to give an address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make a speech' rounds off the surface (and hints at orating) without adding letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of lyric and love poetry in Greek myth.

parts.note: a trench is a ditch
an ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: An energetic labourer digging a ditch.
explanation.definitionFit: Trenchant means incisive and forceful, as in vigorous criticism.

parts.note: reads as preparing a meal or tennis shot, but means signing up for armed service

explanation.surface: A cook prepares to dish up a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist is to join the armed forces, putting oneself in line for military service.

parts.note: the nursery rhyme's twinkling little things are small celestial bodies, here young actresses

explanation.definitionFit: Starlets are young actresses hoping for stardom, and literally little stars that twinkle.
